blocks.content: Comments feel helpful. We are taught early that good developers comment their code. But here is the uncomfortable truth: most comments are noise, and some are actively harmful.
A comment that repeats the code adds clutter. A comment that drifts out of date becomes a lie. The goal is not more comments. It is the right comments.
1. The Best Comment is Often No Comment
blocks.text: 1. The Best Comment is Often No Comment

blocks.content: Before you write a comment, try to make the code say it instead. A clear name or a small function usually beats a sentence of explanation.
A comment is an apology for code that could not explain itself. First try to remove the need for the apology.
2. Comment the Why, Not the What
blocks.text: 2. Comment the Why, Not the What

blocks.content: Good code already shows what it does. What it cannot show is why. The reasons, the history, the tradeoffs, those live only in your head until you write them down.
When you come back in six months you will not wonder what the line does. You will wonder why that strange number is there. Answer that question.
3. When a Comment Earns Its Place
blocks.text: 3. When a Comment Earns Its Place

blocks.content: Some comments are genuinely valuable. Reach for one when the code alone cannot carry the message:

["Why a non obvious decision was made","A warning about a consequence, such as \"changing this breaks the cache\"","The intent behind a tricky algorithm or a dense regular expression","Public API documentation that explains how to use a function","A clearly marked TODO or FIXME that includes real context"]
items: A warning about a consequence, such as "changing this breaks the cache"
The intent behind a tricky algorithm or a dense regular expression
Public API documentation that explains how to use a function
A clearly marked TODO or FIXME that includes real context

blocks.content: If a comment tells the reader something the code cannot, keep it. If it just repeats the code, delete it.
4. Comments That Hurt
blocks.text: 4. Comments That Hurt

blocks.content: These are the comments to hunt down and remove. Each one quietly makes the codebase worse:
Redundant comments
blocks.text: Redundant comments

blocks.content: If the comment says exactly what the next line says, it is pure noise that the reader has to skip over every time.
Commented out code
blocks.text: Commented out code

blocks.content: Do not keep dead code in comments "just in case". Your version control already remembers every old line. Delete it and trust git.
Misleading comments
blocks.text: Misleading comments

blocks.content: A comment that no longer matches the code is worse than no comment, because it actively sends the reader in the wrong direction.
5. Keep Comments Honest
blocks.text: 5. Keep Comments Honest

blocks.content: A comment is a promise, and code changes break promises. When you edit a line, read the comment above it and update it in the same breath.
An out of date comment is a trap. The reader trusts it, the code does something else, and the bug that follows is your fault, not theirs.
Treat a comment like part of the code. If you change the code and leave the comment stale, you have shipped a bug.
6. Common Questions
blocks.text: 6. Common Questions

blocks.content: Should every function have a comment? No. A well named function with clear code needs nothing. Save documentation comments for public APIs and genuinely tricky logic.

Are comments a sign of bad code? Sometimes. If you need a comment to explain what a block does, that block often wants a better name or to become its own function. Comments that explain why are a different and healthy thing.
What about TODO comments? Useful when they carry context and an owner. A bare "TODO fix this" that sits for two years is just guilt on the screen. Be specific or make a ticket.

Is documentation the same as commenting? Related but not identical. API documentation explains how to use code from the outside. Inline comments explain why the code reads the way it does on the inside. Both are useful in their place.
Write code that barely needs comments, then add the few that explain the things code never can. That is the whole craft of commenting.
7. Documentation Comments for Public APIs
blocks.text: 7. Documentation Comments for Public APIs

blocks.content: A documentation comment is a different animal from an inline comment. It is written for someone who will never read the body of your function, only its signature and the comment above it. Javadoc in Java, docstrings in Python, and JSDoc in JavaScript all serve the same purpose: they let a caller understand how to use a piece of code without opening it.
What a good documentation comment includes
blocks.text: What a good documentation comment includes

blocks.content: A useful doc comment answers the questions a caller actually has: what does this do, what do I pass in, what do I get back, and what can go wrong. It rarely needs to explain how the function works internally, that is what the body and its inline comments are for.

codes.python:
def apply_discount(price, discount_percent):
    """Calculate the discounted price for a customer order.

    Args:
        price: the original price before any discount.
        discount_percent: the discount to apply, between 0 and 100.

    Returns:
        The price after the discount is applied.

    Raises:
        ValueError: if discount_percent is outside 0 to 100.
    """
    if discount_percent < 0 or discount_percent > 100:
        raise ValueError('discount_percent must be between 0 and 100')
    return price * (1 - discount_percent / 100)

blocks.content: Notice what this comment does not do. It does not describe the if check inside the function line by line. It describes the contract: the inputs, the output, and the one failure case a caller needs to know about. That contract is exactly what shows up in an IDE tooltip or a generated API reference page.

["State what the function does in one sentence, from the caller perspective","Document every parameter, including the valid range or expected format","Document the return value, including any special cases such as null or empty","Document the exceptions or errors a caller should be ready to handle","Skip internal implementation detail, that belongs inside the function, not above it"]
items: State what the function does in one sentence, from the caller perspective
Document every parameter, including the valid range or expected format
Document the return value, including any special cases such as null or empty
Document the exceptions or errors a caller should be ready to handle
Skip internal implementation detail, that belongs inside the function, not above it

blocks.content: A documentation comment describes a contract. An inline comment explains a decision. Keep the two jobs separate.
8. Inline Comments for Tricky Internal Logic
blocks.text: 8. Inline Comments for Tricky Internal Logic

blocks.content: Not every piece of logic can be made obvious through naming alone. Some algorithms are inherently dense: bit manipulation, a clever mathematical shortcut, a regular expression, or a workaround for a quirky third party API. In these cases a short inline comment earns its keep by translating the trick into plain language.
Keep inline comments close to the code they explain
blocks.text: Keep inline comments close to the code they explain

blocks.content: An inline comment should sit directly above the line or block it clarifies, not in a header far away. The reader should never have to scroll to connect a comment with the code it describes.
Keep inline comments short
blocks.text: Keep inline comments short

blocks.content: One or two lines is usually enough. If the explanation is growing into a paragraph, that is often a sign the logic itself deserves a well named helper function, with the comment becoming the function name instead.

codes.python:
def count_set_bits(n):
    # n & (n - 1) clears the lowest set bit of n
    # this lets us count set bits in O(number of set bits) instead of
    # looping over every one of the 32 or 64 bits
    count = 0
    while n != 0:
        n = n & (n - 1)
        count += 1
    return count

blocks.content: The trick, clearing the lowest set bit with n and n minus one, is not something most readers will recognize on sight. A two line comment turns a clever line into a well understood one, without slowing down everyone who already knows the trick, since they can simply skip past it.
9. When a Comment Is a Signal to Refactor
blocks.text: 9. When a Comment Is a Signal to Refactor

blocks.content: Sometimes the urge to write a comment is really a signal that the code itself is not clear enough. Before you type the comment, run it through two quick tests.
The extract function test
blocks.text: The extract function test

blocks.content: If you are about to write a comment that summarizes a whole block, such as "validate the order before charging the card", stop. That sentence is very close to a perfect function name. Extract the block into a function called validateOrderBeforeCharging and delete the comment, the name now carries the summary permanently.
The rename test
blocks.text: The rename test

blocks.content: If your comment explains what a variable or parameter represents, such as "n is the number of retries remaining", stop. Rename n to retriesRemaining and delete the comment. The information moves from a sentence that can drift out of date into a name that cannot.
If you can imagine deleting a comment by renaming something or extracting a function, do that first. Only keep the comment if no name could carry the same meaning.
10. Before and After: From Comment to Clarity
blocks.text: 10. Before and After: From Comment to Clarity

blocks.content: Here is a small function that mixes both problems this lesson warns about: a redundant comment that only restates the code, and a missing comment where a genuine business rule is actually invisible.
Before: a redundant comment, and a hidden reason
blocks.text: Before: a redundant comment, and a hidden reason

blocks.content: The variable x hides what the value represents, the comments only repeat what the if statement already says, and the real reason for the surcharge, a regulatory requirement, is nowhere to be found.
After: a clear name, and one comment worth keeping
blocks.text: After: a clear name, and one comment worth keeping

blocks.content: Renaming x to transactionAmount and pulling the magic numbers into named constants removes the need for the two "what" comments entirely. In their place is a single comment that explains why the surcharge exists at all, a fact that no amount of clever naming could express.

codes.python:
LARGE_TRANSFER_THRESHOLD = 5000
LARGE_TRANSFER_SURCHARGE = 250

def process_payment(transaction_amount, total):
    # RBI mandates an additional verification fee on transfers above the
    # threshold, to cover the cost of the extra fraud check
    if transaction_amount > LARGE_TRANSFER_THRESHOLD:
        total = total + LARGE_TRANSFER_SURCHARGE
    return total

blocks.title: What changed
blocks.text: Two redundant comments were deleted because better names made them unnecessary. One new comment was added, and it earns its place because it captures a regulatory reason that the code, however well named, simply cannot express on its own.

blocks.content: 11. Comment Guidelines Checklist
blocks.text: 11. Comment Guidelines Checklist

blocks.content: Run through this list before you commit a change that adds or edits a comment.

["Delete any comment that only restates what the very next line already says","Keep any comment that explains why, a workaround, a business rule, or a non obvious tradeoff","Write documentation comments for every public function, class, and API endpoint","Write inline comments only for logic that stays dense even after good naming","Never leave commented out code behind, trust version control to remember it instead","Update or delete a comment in the same commit that changes the code beneath it","Give every TODO an owner and a reason, or turn it into a tracked ticket","Prefer renaming a variable or extracting a function over writing an explanatory comment"]
items: Delete any comment that only restates what the very next line already says
Keep any comment that explains why, a workaround, a business rule, or a non obvious tradeoff
Write documentation comments for every public function, class, and API endpoint
Write inline comments only for logic that stays dense even after good naming
Never leave commented out code behind, trust version control to remember it instead
Update or delete a comment in the same commit that changes the code beneath it

12. The Cost and Value of Comments
blocks.text: 12. The Cost and Value of Comments

blocks.content: Comments are not free. Every comment is a second copy of an idea that now has to be kept in sync with the first copy, the code. Used well, that cost buys real clarity. Used carelessly, it buys confusion later.

{"pros":["Captures reasons, history, and tradeoffs that code cannot express on its own","Turns a public function into something usable without reading its body","Warns future maintainers about non obvious side effects before they get hurt"],"cons":["Can drift out of date and quietly start lying about what the code does","Often papers over a name or structure that should have been improved instead","Adds reading overhead when it only restates code that was already clear"]}

blocks.title: Rule of thumb
blocks.content: If you are unsure whether a comment is worth its cost, ask what happens if you delete it. If a future reader would lose real information, keep it. If they would lose nothing, cut it.
13. Closing the Clean Code for LLD Module
blocks.text: 13. Closing the Clean Code for LLD Module

blocks.content: Naming, structure, and comments are the same idea approached from three directions. A good name removes the need for a comment. A well structured function, small and single purpose, makes its own behavior obvious at a glance. A comment is what is left over for the small handful of things that naming and structure genuinely cannot carry: the why behind a decision, the contract of a public API, and the occasional warning about a trap.

When you sit down in an interview or a real codebase and reach for a comment, pause for a moment first. Ask whether a better name would remove the need for it, whether the block wants to become its own function, and only after that, whether the comment is explaining a why that truly has nowhere else to live. That habit, built up across naming, structure, and commenting, is what separates code that reads like a story from code that reads like a puzzle.
Clean code is not the code with the most comments. It is the code that needed the fewest, because everything else already explained itself.
